title: Boniface and the oak
hook: an English monk fells a sacred oak in Germany and the mission grows; he's martyred in 754
tomorrow: John of Damascus and the icons

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bede, who kept dictating until the last sentence was written. Your line was finishing. What small thing did you finish? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A huge old oak stands at a place called Geismar, in the land of Hesse. People gather there. They honor the tree as holy, the dwelling of a god. And one day a bishop from England, a monk by training, walks up to it with an axe, while a crowd watches and, the story says, curses him under its breath. He begins to cut. The question hanging in the air is simple. If this tree belongs to a god, what happens to the man who strikes it? Today, Boniface and the oak.
screen: `AN OAK AT GEISMAR.` → `A MONK WITH AN AXE.` → `A CROWD WAITING.`

segments.voice: Our account comes from Willibald, a priest who wrote the life of Boniface using what Boniface's companions told him. Boniface was born in England, became a monk, and chose to leave home to preach among the peoples east of the Rhine; by the time of the oak, Willibald says, the pope had made him a bishop. Next, the oak. Willibald says some people in Hesse had been baptized but still honored the old sacred places, and one of those was a great oak. Boniface, with his companions, began to cut it down. Willibald says that after only a little cutting, a great wind shook the tree, and it crashed to the ground and broke apart into four pieces. The people who had cursed him, he says, stopped cursing and began to bless God. Then, what he built. Boniface used the timber of the oak to build a small chapel, dedicated to Saint Peter. The wood of the old worship became the walls of the new. Now the honest part. Willibald tells this as a victory, and that is how the story has been handed down. Some readers today also feel the loss: a tree that people loved, cut down in front of them. Both can be held. The story is about one man's courage, and also about how a people's old faith gave way. Boniface's mission grew. He organized churches and monasteries in Germany. Willibald says that years later, in Frisia, he was killed by attackers while waiting to confirm new Christians, and that he told his companions not to fight back. Catholics honor him as a saint and martyr. The carry is the moment the crowd stopped breathing: the oak fell.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take down one idol. Not someone else's. One of your own. In the Bible's language, an idol is something given more trust than it can bear. A phone checked every few minutes. A number in a bank account. Someone's approval. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself, gently, what has grown too tall in your life. Don't cut it down in anger. Just name it, and notice the hold it has. If you pray, you can hand that hold to God for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Boniface and the oak. An English monk cuts down a sacred tree in Hesse, it falls and breaks, and he builds a chapel from its wood. Today's word.
Your line: the oak fell. Today, when the thing you named reaches for your attention, put it down once, on purpose, and notice that nothing falls on you. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr, and churches in Germany are dedicated to him; the oak of Geismar is told as part of his story.

fork.setup: you're Boniface. people who were baptized still honor a sacred oak, and a crowd is watching. what do you do?

cut the oak down in front of everyone.
go somewhere the old faith isn't so strong.
fork.reveal: he cut it. Willibald says a wind brought it down, it broke in pieces, and Boniface built a chapel from the wood.

original.note: Latin: the oak of Jupiter — Willibald's name for the tree, using a Roman god's name for a Germanic one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary chopping down a tree.
what it means: a test in front of a crowd: the oak fell, and its wood became a chapel.
what a scholar hears: Willibald, writing from the memories of Boniface's companions, calls it the oak of Jupiter and tells it as a turning point.

notes: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii ch. 6: the 'robur Jovis' at Gaesmere; a divine wind; the tree splits into four parts; the oratory to Saint Peter built from its timber. Paraphrased; confirm chapter numbers and details, including 'four pieces'.
Willibald ch. 8: martyrdom in Frisia while awaiting neophytes for confirmation; Boniface forbids resistance. Confirm.
Year of martyrdom (754, in the outline hook) left out of voice under the claims rule.
'Not long after his death' and 'using what Boniface's companions told him': Willibald says he wrote from the accounts of Boniface's disciples. Confirm.
The passage acknowledging the loss felt by those who honored the oak is offered so the older religion is not used as a foil; Keeper to confirm the balance.
Christmas-tree legend attributed to Boniface is later; confirm the myth reveal.
Original: Latin 'robur Jovis'; the Germanic god is often identified as Donar/Thor, not stated here. Confirm pronunciation.
Editor: cut the uncited timing 'not long after his death'; replaced 'Catholics remember it that way' (a claim about all Catholics) with how the story has been handed down.
